result.summary: The Greeks gather at Aulis, where an omen of a serpent and sparrows and the sacrifice of Iphigenia let the fleet sail to Troy. A description of the house of Fame follows. Back at Troy, Protesilaüs falls to Hector, and Achilles fights the invulnerable Cygnus, son of Neptune, strangles him with his helmet straps, and sees him turn into a swan.

scenes.title: Prelude: fleet, Cygnus, Paris
scenes.summary: Overview of the gathering at Aulis, Iphigenia, and the early fighting at Troy, with Priam mourning Cygnus (Æsacus) and Paris bringing war.

scenes.title: The serpent omen at Aulis
scenes.summary: A serpent devours eight young birds and their mother in a plane tree, then turns to stone. Calchas reads it as nine years of war before Troy falls.
scenes.stakes: The Greek expedition needs a sign of whether it will succeed.

scenes.title: Iphigenia is sacrificed
scenes.summary: Contrary winds persist. Calchas declares that Diana must be appeased with a virgin's blood. Iphigenia is brought to the altar, Diana substitutes a hind, and the fleet sails to Phrygia.
scenes.stakes: Iphigenia's life, and the fleet's chance to sail.

scenes.title: The house of Fame
scenes.summary: Ovid describes Fame's brazen house between earth, sea and sky, full of noise and rumours that grow as they travel. Fame announces the coming Greek fleet to the Trojans.

scenes.title: Landing and Achilles meets Cygnus
scenes.summary: The Trojans resist the landing, and Hector kills Protesilaüs. Achilles seeks Cygnus or Hector, finds Cygnus, and throws his spear.
scenes.stakes: Achilles risks his reputation; the Trojans risk losing their line.

scenes.title: The invulnerable Cygnus
scenes.summary: Cygnus boasts that his father Neptune makes him unwoundable. Achilles' spears fail, and he kills Menœtes to test his strength, but Cygnus bears only Menœtes' blood.
scenes.stakes: Achilles' pride and his belief in his own strength.

scenes.title: Cygnus strangled and changed
scenes.summary: Achilles fights on foot, beats Cygnus back, throws him over a stone, and strangles him with his helmet straps. When he moves to strip the body, Neptune turns Cygnus into a white bird.

alias_notes.explanation: Another name for the moon goddess Diana.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid image of Fame's house as a brazen echoing chamber.
Captures how rumour grows with each telling.

analysis.text: Ovid links the Trojan War to omens, sacrifice and rumour, showing events driven by fate, divine anger and Fame's spreading of stories.
The house of Fame draws on Virgil's Fama in the Aeneid and in turn shaped later medieval visions of Fame.

legacy.text: Ovid's house of Fame inspired Chaucer's poem The House of Fame (c. 1379).
The sacrifice of Iphigenia inspired Euripides' plays, and later operas such as Gluck's Iphigénie en Aulide (1774).

fun_facts.text: Ovid's Fame passage resembles the Fama of Virgil's Aeneid, though Ovid makes her house a place of rumour rather than a monster.

language_notes.text: Hector made offerings at an empty tomb (a cenotaph) bearing Cygnus's name, since Cygnus was not dead but a swan.
Pelasgian is used here as a poetic name for the Greeks in general; the Pelasgians were an ancient pre-Greek people.
Bœotian means belonging to Bœotia, the region of central Greece where Aulis lay.
"Dam" means the mother bird; "twice four" means eight, so with the mother there are nine birds.
The nine birds stand for nine years: each bird is one year of war, so Troy falls in the tenth.
Nereus is a sea god, used here for the sea itself. Neptune and Apollo built Troy's walls for King Laomedon, hence Neptune's supposed favour toward Troy.
The son of Thestor is Calchas, the Greek seer, who interprets the omens and names the price of fair winds.
The long sentence builds up to its main verb, 'was appeased', which comes only after the sacrifice scene is set. The hind is a female deer.
Phœbe is Diana, the moon goddess and huntress, whose anger had held the fleet at Aulis. 'Astern' means blowing from behind the ships.
The 'threefold universe' means earth, sea and heaven, whose meeting point is Fame's dwelling.
'The fickle vulgar' means the common, changeable crowd of rumours and gossips.
Protesilaüs was fated to be the first Greek to die at Troy, as an oracle had foretold; Hector kills him here.
Hector is reserved for the tenth year: Achilles will not kill Hector until the last year of the ten-year war.
Hæmonian means Thessalian; Hæmonia is an old name for Thessaly, Achilles' homeland.
Grandson of Æacus: Achilles, whose father Peleus was Æacus's son.
Achilles' mother Thetis was a Nereid, a sea nymph. Cygnus claims a mightier parent, Neptune, who rules the sea and Nereus.
Circus: the Roman arena, where bulls were provoked with cloth. The comparison is anachronistic for Troy.
Lyrnessus, Tenedos and Thebes are towns near Troy that Achilles sacked earlier in the war.
Telephus, king of Mysia, was wounded by Achilles' spear and later healed by its rust. This is why he felt it twice.
The text shifts abruptly between tenses and speakers; the 'he' who is thrown is Cygnus, not Achilles.

context_notes.text: Jupiter, king of the gods, received sacrifices before voyages and campaigns; the altar at Aulis was meant to secure his favour for the fleet.
Calchas was the Greek army's chief seer, who interpreted omens. He is also the one who demands Iphigenia's sacrifice.
Iphigenia was the daughter of Agamemnon, king of Mycenae. He was commander of the Greek fleet, so he had to choose between the army and his child.
Jupiter is the king of the gods and controls thunder and storm clouds.
Sigæum was a headland near Troy, where the Greek ships landed.
Menœtes is a Lycian fighter, one of the Trojan allies.
Cygnus means 'swan' in Greek, so his transformation into a swan fits his name.

literary_notes.text: Repeated "together" stresses the gathering of a whole people behind Paris's act, and the scale of the coming war.
The nine birds devoured foretell the nine years of war that Calchas will read from the omen.
The serpent turned to stone is a fixed sign: the unmoving rock records the omen and the fated length of the war.
The phrase 'is said to have' distances the narrator from the miraculous substitution, as if reporting a tradition he does not vouch for.
'It is all... it is all' and the echoing verbs imitate the house's ceaseless reverberation.
Fame's murmur is compared to distant waves and to fading thunder, which gives the unseen sound a vivid, natural image.
Abstractions such as Credulity, Mistake, Joy and Fears are given a place in the hall as figures, which shows what feeds rumour.
Fame acts as a person who sees and announces, so rumour is shown as an active agent in the war.
Achilles' frustration is compared to a bull goaded by a cloth it cannot hurt, showing his fury and futile strikes.
Achilles doubts his own hand, showing how unsettled even the greatest warrior is by an enemy he cannot wound.
Achilles rejoices at blood that belongs to Menœtes, so his apparent success is a false one.
The final transformation fulfils the hint in Cygnus's name, which was given early and had no stated meaning then.
